about: Mobile- und Servicerobotik 1 (MUS, 2nd semester) and 2 (MUS2, 3rd semester), FH Technikum Wien master's programme, after the slides of Wöber (2018, 2019, 2019a, 2021), the MUS 1 cheat sheet (Wöber 2020) and the convolutional networks slides of Thalhammer (2021). Pages are the PDF pages of each slide file, read in their text layer with pdftotext on 2 Nov 2026; equations shown only as images (the algorithm boxes after Thrun et al. 2006, the HSV and CNN examples) were read from page renderings. The course prints no worked numerical results except the network summary of the CNN slides (p. 10), so those counts are the only printed answers; the MUS Theoriefragen and the 2018 quizzes are questions in words. Every other answer was worked by hand from the course's equations and says so. tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes every answer with the core and fails if they disagree.

lectures.title: The Bayes filter and its family
Robot vision: from pixels to pose

labs.title: Where am I? The Bayes filter on a corridor
labs.idea: Hold a belief over every place the robot could be. Moving blurs it, a reading sharpens it: Bayes' rule in every cell, normalised so it sums to one.

equations.note: Bayes' rule
equations.ref: Basics.pdf, p. 9, eq. 5; MuS1_Cheatsheet.pdf, p. 2, eq. 4

equations.tex: p(d \mid s) = \frac{p(s \mid d)\, p(d)}{p(s \mid d)\, p(d) + p(s \mid \neg d)\, p(\neg d)}
equations.note: The door estimated from one sensor reading
Prediction: the motion model; the integral becomes a sum for countable states (p. 9)
equations.ref: Basics.pdf, p. 21, line 3 (after Thrun et al. 2006)

equations.note: Correction: the sensor model; η normalises

equations.tex: p(x_t \mid u_{1:t}, z_{1:t}) = p(x_t \mid u_t, z_t)
equations.note: Markov assumption: everything needed is in the last state

practice.question: A door sensor sees a door in front of a door with p(s|d) = 0.6 and in front of a wall with p(s|¬d) = 0.3; before reading, door and wall are equally likely. It reports a door. How likely is it a door now?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Basics.pdf, p. 10 (the numbers are an example, not the course's)

practice.question: A corridor of 20 cells has doors in 4 of them. Starting with a flat belief, the same sensor (0.6 and 0.3) reports a door. What is the belief in one door cell now?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Basics.pdf, p. 21, line 4
practice.solution: Each door cell gets 0.6/20, each wall cell 0.3/20; the sum is (4·0.6 + 16·0.3)/20 = 7.2/20. Normalised, a door cell holds 0.6/7.2 = 0.0833.

labs.lecture: Wöber (2018), MuS 1 Basics, pp. 7–21 (Basics.pdf); Wöber (2020), MuS 1 cheat sheet (MuS1_Cheatsheet.pdf)

labs.title: The Kalman filter: trust the model or the sensor?
labs.idea: With Gaussians everywhere and a linear model, the Bayes filter becomes the Kalman filter: a mean and a variance, predicted by the motion and corrected by the measurement, weighed by the Kalman gain.
labs.lawTex: K_t = \bar\Sigma_t C_t^{\mathsf T} \left(C_t \bar\Sigma_t C_t^{\mathsf T} + Q_t\right)^{-1}

equations.note: Prediction of the mean (the slide's p. 6 writes Axt−1 − But; eq. 2 on p. 7 and the algorithm have +)
Prediction of the covariance: the + R makes it grow

equations.tex: K_t = \bar\Sigma_t C_t^{\mathsf T} \left(C_t \bar\Sigma_t C_t^{\mathsf T} + Q_t\right)^{-1}
equations.note: The Kalman gain: a large sensor noise Q makes it small
Correction of the mean by the innovation
Correction of the covariance

equations.eq: xt = A·xt−1 + B·ut + εt, zt = C·xt + δt
equations.tex: x_t = A x_{t-1} + B u_t + \varepsilon_t,\quad z_t = C x_t + \delta_t
equations.note: εt ∼ N(0, R) the process noise, δt ∼ N(0, Q) the sensor noise

practice.question: One step of a scalar Kalman filter, A = B = C = 1: μ = 0, Σ = 1, u = 1, R = 0.5, Q = 1, z = 1.2. What is the Kalman gain K?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gaussianfilters.pdf, pp. 11–13

practice.question: Same step: what is the corrected variance Σ?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Gaussianfilters.pdf, p. 13, line 6
practice.solution: Σ = (1 − 0.6)·1.5 = 0.6: smaller than both Σ̄ = 1.5 and Q = 1.

labs.title: Odometry: from wheel turns to a path
labs.idea: Count the turns of the two wheels of a differential drive and the robot's step follows: half their sum gives the distance, their difference over the track gives the turn.

equations.note: Distance of one step, r the wheel radius
Turn of one step, b the track width (baseline)

equations.eq: (X, Y, θ)t = (X, Y, θ)t−1 + (δd·cos(θt−1 + δθ), δd·sin(θt−1 + δθ), δθ)
equations.note: The pose moved by one step: not linear in θ, hence the EKF

equations.eq: ICR = (x − L·sin θ, y + L·cos θ)
equations.note: The instantaneous centre of rotation, L from the robot's centre
Turning radius, speed over turn rate; worked here, not on the slides

labs.title: The EKF: an ellipse for a banana
labs.idea: The motion bends, a Gaussian cannot: the EKF linearises the motion at the mean with its Jacobian and gets an ellipse, while sampled poses spread into a curved cloud.

equations.eq: xt = g(ut, xt−1) + εt, zt = h(xt) + δt
equations.note: A and B replaced by g(.), C by h(.)

equations.eq: g(ut, xt−1) ≈ g(ut, μt−1) + Gt(xt−1 − μt−1)
equations.note: First-order Taylor series at the mean; Gt the Jacobian

equations.eq: μ̄t = g(ut, μt−1), Σ̄t = Gt·Σt−1·Gtᵀ + Rt
equations.note: The EKF's prediction
The Jacobian of the odometry step, worked here from EKF.pdf, p. 3, eq. 1

equations.tex: R_t = V_t \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_d^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_\theta^2 \end{pmatrix} V_t^{\mathsf T},\quad V_t = \frac{\partial g}{\partial(\delta_d, \delta_\theta)}
equations.note: The noise of δd and δθ carried into x, y, θ; worked here so the EKF and the samples share one noise

practice.question: At θ = 0, a step with δd = 0.5 m and δθ = 30°: what is the entry G13 = ∂x/∂θ of the Jacobian?
practice.source: Worked by hand from EKF.pdf, p. 3, eq. 1

practice.question: Heading north (θ = 90°, 1.5708 rad), the robot drives 1 m straight on. What is G13 now?
practice.source: Worked by hand from EKF.pdf, p. 3, eq. 1
practice.solution: −1·sin 90° = −1: an error in the heading moves the robot sideways in x by the full distance driven.

labs.lecture: Wöber (2018), MuS 1 Extended Kalman Filter, pp. 3–12 (EKF.pdf); Wöber (2021), MuS 1 Partikelfilter, pp. 5 and 20 (MCMC.pdf)

labs.title: Monte Carlo localisation: many guesses at once
labs.idea: Let hundreds of particles each guess where the robot is. Move them with noise, weight them by how well each explains the reading, and redraw them in proportion to their weights: the guesses that fit survive.
labs.law: wt[m] = p(zt | xt[m]); draw M particles with probability ∝ wt[m]

equations.note: Sampling from a proposal q and weighting by rl = p/q
Prediction: sample each particle's move from the motion model
Weight by the sensor model

equations.eq: draw i with probability ∝ wt[i], with replacement, M times
equations.note: Resampling, the correction step
A normal distribution as sensor model, ẑ the reading the particle expects
equations.ref: MCMC.pdf, p. 19; Basics.pdf, p. 14, eq. 9 in one dimension

practice.question: A range sensor with σ = 1 m reads z = 3 m. A particle expects ẑ = 1 m. What is its unnormalised weight exp(−(z − ẑ)²/(2σ²))?
practice.source: Worked by hand from MCMC.pdf, p. 19
practice.solution: exp(−2²/2) = e⁻² = 0.135: two standard deviations off, against 1 for a particle that expects exactly 3 m.

practice.question: Same reading, σ = 0.5 m, a particle expecting ẑ = 2.5 m: its weight?
practice.source: Worked by hand from MCMC.pdf, p. 19
practice.solution: exp(−0.5²/(2·0.25)) = e^−0.5 = 0.607: one standard deviation off.

labs.title: Denoising: box, median and Gaussian
labs.idea: Slide a small window over the image and replace each pixel by its window's mean, weighted mean or median: noise falls, and edges blur unless the median keeps them.
labs.law: g(i, j) = Σk,l I(i + k, j + l)·h(k, l)
labs.lawTex: g(i, j) = \sum_{k,l} I(i + k,\, j + l)\, h(k, l)

equations.eq: g(i, j) = Σk,l I(i + k, j + l)·h(k, l)
equations.tex: g(i, j) = \sum_{k,l} I(i + k,\, j + l)\, h(k, l)
equations.note: The kernel slid over the image (the slide calls it convolution; written this way it is a correlation, the same for symmetric kernels)
The normalised box filter

equations.eq: p̃ = p(n+1)/2 for n odd, (pn/2 + p1+n/2)/2 for n even
equations.tex: \tilde p = \begin{cases} p_{(n+1)/2} & n \text{ odd} \\ \tfrac12\left(p_{n/2} + p_{1+n/2}\right) & n \text{ even} \end{cases}
equations.note: The median of the sorted window
The Gaussian filter, a box weighted by the Gauss bell, normalised to sum to one
equations.ref: 1_Entrauschen.pdf, p. 9; the bell from Basics.pdf, p. 14, eq. 9

practice.question: A 3 × 3 window holds 12, 200, 15 / 14, 255, 13 / 16, 0, 15. What does the median filter put in its centre?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 1_Entrauschen.pdf, p. 8, eq. 3
practice.solution: Sorted: 0, 12, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 200, 255; n = 9, the 5th value is 15. The stuck pixels 0 and 255 have no effect.

practice.question: The same window through the 3 × 3 box filter: what is the centre value?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 1_Entrauschen.pdf, p. 7, eq. 2
practice.solution: (12 + 200 + 15 + 14 + 255 + 13 + 16 + 0 + 15)/9 = 540/9 = 60: the stuck pixels pull it far from the 15 around it.

labs.title: Thresholds, colour indices and Otsu
labs.idea: Cut an image into object and background with a threshold. A colour index makes the object stand out first; Otsu's idea lets the image choose the threshold that separates two classes of grey values best.

equations.note: A fixed threshold
The excess colour index; p. 11 uses 2Ib − Ir − Ig for blue
The criterion the slide gives for Otsu's method (Fisher's discriminant); the best TH maximises it

equations.eq: pj ∈ C1 if pj ≤ TH, C2 if pj > TH
equations.tex: p_j \in \begin{cases} C_1 & p_j \le T_H \\ C_2 & p_j > T_H \end{cases}
equations.note: The two classes, TH tried from 0 to 255

labs.title: HSV: colour as hue, saturation and value
labs.idea: Turn red, green and blue into a hue angle, a saturation and a brightness, and a colour is found by its hue alone, whatever the lighting does to the three channels.
labs.lawTex: H = \begin{cases} 60^\circ\,\frac{I_g - I_b}{\Delta} & C_{\max} = I_r \\ 60^\circ\left(2 + \frac{I_b - I_r}{\Delta}\right) & C_{\max} = I_g \\ 60^\circ\left(4 + \frac{I_r - I_g}{\Delta}\right) & C_{\max} = I_b \end{cases}

equations.eq: Cmax = max(Ir, Ig, Ib), Cmin = min(…), Δ = Cmax − Cmin
equations.tex: C_{\max} = \max(I_r, I_g, I_b),\quad C_{\min} = \min(I_r, I_g, I_b),\quad \Delta = C_{\max} - C_{\min}
equations.note: The extremes

equations.eq: H = 0 if Δ = 0; 60°·(Ig − Ib)/Δ if Cmax = Ir; 60°·(2 + (Ib − Ir)/Δ) if Cmax = Ig; 60°·(4 + (Ir − Ig)/Δ) if Cmax = Ib
equations.tex: H = \begin{cases} 0 & \Delta = 0 \\ 60^\circ\,\frac{I_g - I_b}{\Delta} & C_{\max} = I_r \\ 60^\circ\left(2 + \frac{I_b - I_r}{\Delta}\right) & C_{\max} = I_g \\ 60^\circ\left(4 + \frac{I_r - I_g}{\Delta}\right) & C_{\max} = I_b \end{cases}
equations.note: Hue, then brought into 0°–360°

equations.eq: S = Δ/Cmax (0 if Cmax = 0), V = Cmax
equations.note: Saturation and value

equations.tex: h = \left\lfloor \frac{H}{60^\circ} \right\rfloor,\ f = \frac{H}{60^\circ} - h,\ p = V(1 - S),\ q = V(1 - Sf),\ t = V(1 - S(1 - f))
equations.note: Back to RGB: the sector and the helper values
For h = 0 to 5; the slide prints (q, V, t) for h = 2, a slip: R must be p there

labs.title: Edges: Sobel and Canny
labs.idea: An edge is where the grey value changes fast. Sobel kernels measure the change in x and y; Canny smooths first, thins each edge to one pixel and keeps weak edges only when they join strong ones.
labs.law: |∇f| = √(fx² + fy²), Gx = Kx ∗ I, Gy = Ky ∗ I

equations.tex: \nabla f(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} \partial f / \partial x \\ \partial f / \partial y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} f'_x \\ f'_y \end{pmatrix}
equations.note: The image gradient
Size and direction; the slide writes atan2(fx, fy), the lab measures θ from the x axis
The central difference, one pixel the smallest step
The Sobel kernels; Gx = Kx ∗ I, Gy = Ky ∗ I
Scaling a gradient image to show it: a gradient of 0 becomes mid grey
Canny's first step, then Sobel, non-maximum suppression (p. 13) and two thresholds (p. 14)

labs.title: A convolution layer, counted
labs.idea: A convolution layer slides the same small kernels over the whole image, adds a bias, and passes the result through ReLU and pooling: few weights, shared everywhere. Count them, and the output's size, the way the network summary does.

labs.title: Depth from a stereo pair
labs.idea: Two cameras a baseline apart see a point at different columns. The nearer the point, the bigger the shift, the disparity: depth is baseline times focal length over disparity.

equations.note: Depth from disparity D, B the baseline, f the focal length; similar triangles

equations.eq: u = fx·xc/zc + cx, v = fy·yc/zc + cy
equations.tex: \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} c_x \\ c_y \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{z_c} \begin{pmatrix} f_x\, x_c \\ f_y\, y_c \end{pmatrix}
equations.note: The pinhole camera with the chip's offset

equations.tex: s \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = K \left[\, R \mid t \,\right] \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
equations.note: Projection with the pose of the object in the camera's frame, the unknown of pose estimation

equations.eq: width in image / f = real width / Z
equations.note: A flat object parallel to the chip

labs.title: RANSAC: fit what most points agree on
labs.idea: Least squares listens to every point, outliers too. RANSAC fits the fewest points a model needs, again and again, keeps the model most points agree with, and only then fits it to those.
labs.law: Θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀY on the inliers of the best two-point line

equations.note: Least squares, here for a line y = kx + d; in pose estimation the direct linear transform

equations.eq: per cycle: 2 random points, fit, count inliers within ε, stop when inliers/n > τ
equations.note: The RANSAC loop for a line; after the stop or N cycles, refit with all inliers

practice.question: Four points (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3) and (3, 10). What slope k does least squares give over all four?
practice.source: Worked by hand from 11_Pose-Estimation.pdf, p. 34, eq. 15
practice.solution: n = 4, Σx = 6, Σy = 16, Σx² = 14, Σxy = 38: k = (4·38 − 6·16)/(4·14 − 36) = 56/20 = 2.8. The one outlier almost triples the slope.
